Rank models by BIC

Source: R/aic_tab.R
bic_tab.Rd

Build a model-selection table ranked by BIC (the Bayesian information criterion) for a list of fitted models. As in aic_tab(), each estimated scale of effect (sigma) and kernel shape counts as a parameter, and lists can mix multiScaleR objects with plain fitted models.

Usage

bic_tab(mod_list,
        mod_names = NULL,
        verbose = FALSE,
        ...)

Arguments

mod_list

A list of fitted models: multiScaleR objects from multiScale_optim(), plain fitted models, or both. Every model must be fitted to the same observations with a comparable likelihood, including matching responses, weights, and likelihood measure. Bayesian fits, cross-validation results, and private spatial prototypes are rejected.

mod_names

Optional character vector of model names, one per model in mod_list. By default, multiScaleR objects are labeled [kernel=...; family=...] followed by the right-hand side of the model formula.

verbose

Logical. If TRUE, the table is also printed to the console. Default FALSE.

...

Not used.

Value

A data frame of class "bictab" (from the AICcmodavg package), sorted from the best (smallest) BIC, with one row per model:

  • Modnames: model name.

  • K: number of estimated parameters, counted as in aic_tab(): the fitted likelihood parameters (including ancillary ones such as negative binomial dispersion, or native effective degrees of freedom for GAMs) plus each estimated scale and shape of a multiScaleR model.

  • BIC: the Bayesian information criterion. Smaller is better.

  • Delta_BIC: difference from the best model.

  • BICWt: BIC weight, the relative support for each model within this set. Weights sum to 1.

  • Cum.Wt: cumulative BIC weight.

  • LL: maximized log-likelihood.

A likelihood_adjustments attribute is added when a likelihood was adjusted, as described in aic_tab().

Details

BIC penalizes each parameter by the log of the sample size rather than by 2, so it penalizes complexity more heavily than AIC once there are more than about 7 observations. It is often preferred when the goal is the single best-supported model rather than model averaging.

Every rule in aic_tab() applies here: the parameter count (including all estimated components of unmarked models, spaMM degrees of freedom, and the checked negative binomial BAM adjustment), the comparability checks (responses, rows, weights, binomial outcomes, ML and REML, partial likelihoods, used pcount() visits, and distance-removal protocols), the sample-size conventions (retained site rows for unmarked models and native event counts for Cox and conditional logistic models), and the rejected models. Inapplicable hard-radius shape positions are excluded from K. Calling the criterion BIC does not make a posterior target a sampling likelihood, so Bayesian fits are rejected here too.

The table itself is built with AICcmodavg::bictabCustom().

See also

aic_tab(), multiScale_optim(), and vignette("v02-user-guide", package = "multiScaleR").

Author

Bill Peterman

Examples

## Bundled counts simulated with a habitat scale of 75 map units
data("pts")
data("count_data")
hab <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata", "hab.tif", package = "multiScaleR"))
prepared <- kernel_prep(pts, hab, max_D = 300, sigma = 75, verbose = FALSE)
dat <- data.frame(y = count_data$y, prepared$kernel_dat)
fixed_model <- glm(y ~ hab, family = poisson(), data = dat)
null_model <- glm(y ~ 1, family = poisson(), data = dat)
spatial_model <- multiScale_optim(fixed_model, prepared, par = 75 / 300,
                                  n_cores = 1, verbose = FALSE)

## BIC charges log(75), about 4.3, for the estimated sigma, versus 2 in AIC
bic_tab(list(spatial_model, fixed_model, null_model),
        mod_names = c("spatial", "fixed", "null"))
#> 
#> Model selection based on BIC:
#> 
#>         K    BIC Delta_BIC BICWt Cum.Wt      LL
#> fixed   2 236.98      0.00   0.9    0.9 -114.17
#> spatial 3 241.29      4.31   0.1    1.0 -114.17
#> null    1 349.01    112.03   0.0    1.0 -172.34
#>
